title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
Slides this post is based on: Lecture 08, Tree Indexes I and Lecture 09, Tree Indexes II from CMU 15-445/645 (Prof. Andy Pavlo).
The ideas come from those slides. The diagrams, examples and analogies are my own, so any mistakes are mine.

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
The problem in one sentence
You have a table with a billion rows and a query that wants one of them. Reading every row is a non-starter. An index is a second, smaller, carefully organized structure that tells the database where to look.
In the previous post we met the buffer pool: a cache of disk pages in memory. Indexes live on top of that. Every node of an index is a page, and every step of a lookup is “ask the buffer pool for that page.” So the real goal of a good index is simple: touch as few pages as possible.
The mental model I will use throughout is the back-of-the-book index. If you want every page that mentions “buffer pool”, you do not read the whole book. You flip to the index, find the word, and jump to the page numbers. Different books (and different questions) need different kinds of index, and that is what this post is about.
Here is the map of what we will cover:



Question you are asking
Structure that answers it
Section




“Give me key = 42, or all keys between 10 and 99”
B+Tree
B+Trees


“Is this key even in the set?” (cheap yes/no)
Bloom filter
Filters


“Ordered keys, in memory, easy concurrency”
Skip list
Skip lists


“Keys that share prefixes (strings, bit patterns)”
Trie / radix tree
Tries


“Which documents contain the word X?”
Inverted index
Inverted indexes


“Which items are similar to this one?”
Vector index
Vector indexes

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
Indexes vs. filters
The lecture draws a line that is easy to miss:









Index
Filter




Answers
“Where is the tuple with this key?”
“Is this key (probably) in the set?”


Returns
A location (record id)
Yes / no


Example
B+Tree
Bloom filter



An index leads you to the data. A filter only tells you whether going to look is worthwhile.

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
The B+Tree

Intuition
Picture a big library. You do not search every shelf. A sign at the entrance says “Fiction left, Science right”. Inside Science, another sign says “A to M this aisle”. At the end of the aisle the shelf is labelled and the books are in order, with each shelf continuing into the next.
A B+Tree is exactly that: a few levels of signs, then sorted data at the bottom, with shelves linked left to right.
The name is a family, by the way: B-Tree (1970), B+Tree (1973), B*Tree, B-link Tree, B-epsilon Tree, Bw-Tree. People often say “B-Tree” to mean any of them, and nearly every database actually ships a B+Tree.


The rules
A B+Tree of fanout \(m\) is a self-balancing, ordered, \(m\)-way tree:

Perfectly balanced. Every leaf is at the same depth, so every lookup costs the same number of page reads.
Half-full rule. Every node except the root holds at least \(\lceil m/2 \rceil - 1\) keys and at most \(m - 1\) keys.
Fanout rule. An inner node with \(k\) keys has exactly \(k + 1\) children.
Ordered. Keys inside a node are sorted, so you can binary-search them.
Logarithmic. Search, insert and delete cost \(O(\log_m n)\).

A tiny example to keep in mind: with \(m = 4\), a node holds 1 to 3 keys (the root may hold fewer). The figures below use that setting.


Anatomy






Figure 1: A small B+Tree. The root and inner nodes hold only separator keys. All real keys and their values sit in the leaves, and the leaves are chained with sibling pointers.



Read Figure 1 top to bottom:

The root key 20 splits the world in two: keys below 20 go left, keys at or above 20 go right.
Inner nodes repeat the idea: 10 splits the left half, 35 splits the right half.
Leaf nodes hold the actual keys and, beside each key, a value.
The orange arrows are sibling pointers. They are what make range scans cheap (more on that in a moment).

Inside each node, the layout is an array of keys with an array of “next steps”: an inner node holds <child page> | key | <child page> | key | ... while a leaf holds key | value | key | value | ....






Figure 2: The layout of one leaf page: a small header (level, how many slots are used, ids of the previous and next leaf, a high key), then the sorted keys and, in parallel, their values.



Two details are worth noticing in Figure 2:

The links are page ids, not memory addresses. The node has to be writable to disk verbatim, so it cannot contain raw pointers. (We will come back to this under “pointer swizzling”.)
NULL keys are usually all parked in the first or last leaf, so they do not confuse comparisons.



What is the “value” in a leaf?
Two common answers:








Approach
What the leaf stores
Notes




Record id
A pointer to the tuple: (page id, slot)
The most common design. The index is separate from the table.


Tuple data
The whole row
This is index-organized storage. For the primary-key index the leaf is the row. Secondary indexes then store the primary key as their value.



With the second approach a lookup through a secondary index is two tree descents: find the primary key in the secondary index, then use it to find the row in the primary index.


B-Tree vs. B+Tree
The original B-Tree stored keys and values in every node, which is more space-efficient because each key appears once. A B+Tree stores values only in leaves; inner nodes are pure signposts.
That sounds like a step backwards, but it pays off: signposts are small, so each inner page fits many more of them. A larger fanout means a shorter tree. And putting every key in the leaf level lets you chain leaves together for scans.


How big is “big”?
Take a 16 KB page. A key plus a child pointer is, say, 16 bytes, so a page could hold about 1,000 entries. Real nodes are not perfectly full. The lecture quotes an average occupancy of about 69%, so call it 700.
\[
\text{entries reachable} \approx 700^{h}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
700^{3} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{8},\quad 700^{4} \approx 2.4 \times 10^{11}
\]
Three levels already index a third of a billion keys; four levels cover a couple of hundred billion. The root and the next level are hit by every query, so they live permanently in the buffer pool. In practice a lookup on a huge table costs about one disk read: the leaf.


Lookups and range scans
Let us trace Figure 1.
Point lookup: find 31.

Root [20]: 31 >= 20, go right.
Inner [35]: 31 < 35, go left.
Leaf [20, 31]: binary-search, found 31. Follow its value to the tuple.

Three pages. That is the cost whether the table has 100 rows or 100 million.
Range scan: WHERE key BETWEEN 10 AND 35.

Descend to the leaf that would contain 10: leaf [10, 15].
Read 10, 15. Hit the end of the leaf, so follow the sibling pointer to [20, 31].
Read 20, 31, follow the pointer to [35, 38, 44].
35 is in range, 38 is not. Stop.

No re-descending from the root, no sorting. That is the entire reason leaves are linked.


Insert
The recipe is short:

Descend to the correct leaf \(L\).
Insert the key into \(L\) in sorted position.
If \(L\) still has room, done.
Otherwise split \(L\): spread its entries over \(L\) and a new node \(L_2\), and add an entry for \(L_2\) to the parent.







flowchart TD
    A["Descend to the target leaf"] --> B{"Room in the leaf?"}
    B -- "yes" --> C["Insert in sorted order. Done."]
    B -- "no" --> D["Split leaf into two halves"]
    D --> E["COPY the first key of the right half up to the parent"]
    E --> F{"Room in the parent?"}
    F -- "yes" --> G["Done."]
    F -- "no" --> H["Split the inner node. PUSH the middle key up"]
    H --> I{"Was it the root?"}
    I -- "no" --> F
    I -- "yes" --> J["Create a new root. Tree grows by one level."]


 B+Tree insert. 









Figure 3: Inserting 6 into a full leaf. The leaf splits in two and the first key of the right half (6) is copied up into the parent.



In Figure 3 the leaf [2, 4, 8] is full (max 3 keys), so inserting 6 would make four. We split into [2, 4] and [6, 8], and the parent gains the signpost 6: “keys from 6 up are in the new right leaf.”

Copy up vs. push up
This is the subtle bit that trips people up:







Splitting
What happens to the middle key




Leaf
Copied up. It must remain in the leaf, because the leaf has to contain every real key.


Inner node
Pushed up (moved). Inner keys are only signposts, so keeping a duplicate one level down would be pointless.





When the tree grows
If the split cascades all the way up and the root itself is full, the root splits and a new root with a single key is created above it. The height goes up by one, and every leaf is still at the same depth. This is why a B+Tree stays balanced for free: it only ever grows from the top, never from the bottom.



Delete
Deletion is insertion in reverse:

Descend to the leaf, remove the entry.
If the leaf is still at least half full, done.
Otherwise it is underfull. First try to borrow an entry from a sibling (same parent) that has one to spare.
If no sibling can spare one, merge the leaf with a sibling and remove the separator from the parent.
The parent lost a key, so it may now be underfull, and the process repeats upward.







flowchart TD
    A["Find the leaf, remove the entry"] --> B{"At least half full?"}
    B -- "yes" --> C["Done."]
    B -- "no" --> D{"Sibling has a spare key?"}
    D -- "yes" --> E["Borrow it. Update the separator in the parent. Done."]
    D -- "no" --> F["Merge with the sibling"]
    F --> G["Remove the separator from the parent"]
    G --> H{"Parent underfull?"}
    H -- "yes" --> D
    H -- "no" --> I["Done."]


 B+Tree delete. 









Figure 4: Delete in action: first a borrow from a “rich” sibling, then a merge when the sibling has nothing to spare.



Walk through Figure 4:

Deleting 2 empties its leaf, which violates “at least 1 key”. The right sibling [6, 8] has two keys, so it can lend one.
We borrow 6. The leaf is now [6], the sibling is [8], and the parent’s separator is updated from 6 to 8 so it still describes the boundary correctly.
Later, deleting 6 empties the leaf again. This time the sibling [8] has exactly the minimum, so it cannot lend. We merge and delete the separator from the parent.

If merges cascade up to the root and the root is left with zero keys, its single remaining child becomes the new root, and the tree shrinks one level. Growing and shrinking both happen at the top, which keeps the leaves level.


Composite (multi-column) indexes
An index can be on several columns, such as (a, b, c). The key is the tuple of those values, compared left to right, like sorting a phone book by last name, then first name, then middle name.
CREATE INDEX my_idx ON t (a, b DESC, c NULLS FIRST);
The ordering you declare (ASC/DESC, where NULLs go) is baked into the tree. The golden rule is the prefix rule: the index helps only if the query constrains a leading prefix of the columns.







Query on index (a, b, c)
Can the tree navigate with it?




a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3
Yes, full key


a = 1 AND b = 2
Yes, prefix (a, b)


a = 1
Yes, prefix (a)


a = 1 AND c = 3
Partly: navigates by a, then c must be filtered afterwards


b = 2
Generally no (the lecture says rarely supported)


c = 3
Generally no



Why does b = 2 fail? Look at the sorted keys of a two-column index (a, b):
(1,1) (1,2) (1,3) | (2,1) (2,2) (2,3) | (3,1) (3,3) | (4,1)
All entries with b = 1 are (1,1) (2,1) (3,1) (4,1): scattered across the whole tree. There is no contiguous range to jump to, so the DBMS cannot use the sort order. The phone-book version: you cannot look up everyone named “Priya” without knowing the last name.
The same logic means column order matters. Put the column you filter by equality most often first.


Duplicate keys
What if you build a non-unique index and many rows share a key? Two approaches:








Approach
How
Trade-off




Append the record id
Make the key (key, rid). Now every key is unique. Searches by the original key still work as a prefix search.
Simple, widely used.


Overflow leaf nodes
When a leaf cannot hold all copies of a key, chain extra overflow pages.
More complex to maintain and modify. The lecture’s advice is “don’t do this.”



There is also an optimization where a leaf stores each key once with a list of values (deduplication), which we will see later.


Clustered indexes and why page order matters
A clustered index means the table’s rows are physically stored in primary-key order. Some systems (MySQL InnoDB, for example) always cluster; if you declare no primary key they invent a hidden one. Others cannot cluster at all.
The payoff is for scans. SELECT * FROM t ORDER BY pk becomes: walk to the leftmost leaf and follow the sibling chain. The data is already sorted on disk, so this beats sorting at query time every time.
A non-clustered index is where it gets ugly. The index returns record ids in key order, but the rows they point to are scattered over many pages. Suppose the index yields tuples living on pages:
102, 103, 102, 104, 103, 101, 104
Fetching in that order may re-read pages (if they were evicted in between). The smarter approach is index scan page sorting: collect all the record ids the query needs first, sort them by page id, then fetch:
101, 102, 102, 103, 103, 104, 104   -> each page is read exactly once
You give up the key order of the output (the optimizer will re-sort if the query demands it) in exchange for far fewer page reads.

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
B+Tree design choices
The rules above leave room for real engineering decisions.

Node size
The slower the storage, the larger the node should be. Slow devices reward big sequential reads, so amortize the cost over many keys.



Storage
Rough optimal node size




Spinning disk (HDD)
~1 MB


SSD
~10 KB


In-memory
~512 B



The “right” number also depends on workload: large leaves favour long scans, small nodes favour root-to-leaf probes.


Merge threshold
Strictly following “merge at half full” can cause thrashing: a node that just merged may split again on the next insert. Many systems delay merging and let nodes stay underfull for a while, rebuilding the whole index occasionally. PostgreSQL’s B+Tree (nbtree) is the standard example: it is lazy about reorganizing, which is why the lecture jokes it is a “non-balanced” B+Tree. The measured average node occupancy of around 69% is partly a consequence of this.


Variable-length keys
Strings and other variable-size keys break the clean “array of fixed slots” picture. Four options:








Approach
Idea
Cost




Pointers
Store the key as a pointer to the real value in the tuple
Extra memory jump per comparison; bad for caches


Variable-length nodes
Let node sizes vary
Tricky memory management


Padding
Pad every key to the maximum length
Wastes space


Key map / indirection
Keep a small array of offsets pointing to keys packed inside the node
The common practical choice





Searching inside a node
Once a page is in memory you still must find the key within it:

Linear scan. Compare from the start. Sounds slow, but with SIMD you compare many keys per instruction (e.g. checking 4 or 8 integers at once), so for small nodes it is very competitive.
Binary search. Jump to the middle, go left or right. \(O(\log_2 k)\) comparisons.
Interpolation. If keys are roughly evenly spread, guess where the key sits, like opening a dictionary near the back when you look up “zebra.” For a sorted array with \(n\) keys between min and max:

\[
\text{position} \approx \frac{\text{target} - \text{min}}{\text{max} - \text{min}} \times (n - 1)
\]
Example: keys 4 5 6 7 8 9 10, looking for 8: \(\frac{8 - 4}{10 - 4} \times 6 = 4\), so jump straight to index 4. It only works well for fairly uniform data.

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
B+Tree optimizations

Pointer swizzling
Nodes refer to their children by page id. Every hop requires the DBMS to look the page id up in the buffer pool’s page table to get a memory address. If a page is pinned in memory (the root and top levels, say), we can store the raw memory pointer in the parent instead and skip the lookup entirely. The cost is bookkeeping: a swizzled pointer is only valid while the page stays in memory, so the DBMS must unswizzle when evicting. This is a direct tie-in to the buffer pool post.


Buffered updates (write-optimized trees)
Splits and merges are expensive, and the unlucky writer who triggers one pays for it. What if updates could be batched?
In a B-epsilon tree (also called a fractal tree), every inner node has a small log buffer. Instead of walking down to the leaf, an insert or delete is appended to the root’s buffer. When a buffer fills up, its messages are flushed one level down, in bulk, and so on. Many changes share one trip down the tree. A lookup must check the buffers on the way down, because the newest value for a key might still be sitting in one.
The trade is classic: faster writes, slightly slower reads.


Partial indexes
Index only a subset of the rows. The index is smaller, cheaper to maintain, and still useful if your queries target that subset:
CREATE INDEX idx_foo ON foo (a, b) WHERE c = 'WuTang';

-- Can use the partial index:
SELECT b FROM foo WHERE a = 123 AND c = 'WuTang';
A common use is one index per time range (per month or per year), so old, rarely queried data does not bloat the hot index.


Included columns (covering indexes)
Sometimes the query needs a column that is not part of the search key. You can include it as extra payload in the leaf only:
CREATE INDEX idx_foo ON foo (a, b) INCLUDE (c);

SELECT b FROM foo WHERE a = 123 AND c = 'WuTang';
Here c is not used to navigate, but it is stored in the leaf. If every column the query needs is in the index, the DBMS never touches the table: an index-only scan (the index is then called a covering index). It saves one random page read per row, which is often the dominant cost.


Prefix compression
Sorted keys in one leaf tend to share beginnings. Store the common prefix once:
robbed  robbing  robot      ->   prefix "rob" + suffixes: bed  bing  ot


Deduplication
For non-unique indexes, avoid storing the same key over and over. Store it once with a posting list of values:
K1 V1 | K1 V2 | K1 V3 | K2 V4     ->     K1 -> [V1, V2, V3] | K2 -> [V4]


Suffix truncation
Inner-node keys only need to be long enough to direct traffic. If the left subtree ends at abcdefghijk and the right begins at lmnopqrstuv, the separator can be just lmn (even l suffices here). Shorter separators mean more of them per page, which means higher fanout, a shorter tree and fewer page reads.


Bulk insert
Building an index on an existing table by inserting rows one at a time does a descent and possibly a split for every row. A far faster approach is to sort the keys first and build bottom-up:
keys:    3  7  9  13  6  1
sorted:  1  3  6  7   9  13

leaf level:     [1 3 6]   [7 9 13]       <- fill leaves left to right, link them
parent level:        [7]                 <- one separator per boundary
No splits, no descents, and the leaves come out tightly packed and sequential on disk.

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
Beyond the B+Tree
Lecture 09 tackles a different question: what about workloads a B+Tree is not good at? Four of them appear below: cheap existence checks, in-memory ordered data, prefix-heavy keys, and searching by content or meaning rather than by value.

Bloom filters and other filters
The problem. In a B+Tree, even asking “does key X exist?” costs a full descent to the leaf, potentially one buffer pool miss per level. If the answer is often “no”, that is wasted I/O.
The idea. A Bloom filter is a tiny bit array plus \(k\) hash functions. It can say “definitely not present” or “probably present”.

Insert\((x)\): hash \(x\) with each of the \(k\) functions and set those bits to 1.
Lookup\((x)\): hash the same way. If any of those bits is 0, \(x\) was never inserted. If all are 1, it is probably present.







Figure 5: A Bloom filter with 8 bits and 2 hash functions. “cow” hits a zero bit, so it is definitely absent. “emu” lands on bits that other keys happened to set, giving a false positive.



Look at Figure 5 carefully:

No false negatives, ever. If a key was inserted, all its bits are 1, so the lookup says “maybe.” The filter cannot forget.
False positives are possible. emu was never inserted, but dog set bit 3 and cat set bit 5. The filter cannot tell whose bits they are.

The false positive rate depends on the number of bits \(m\), the number of inserted keys \(n\) and the number of hash functions \(k\):
\[
p \approx \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^{k}
\]
Give it more bits per key and the rate drops fast. About 10 bits per key with a good choice of \(k\) gets you near 1%. Crucially, the filter is small enough to sit in memory, so a “definitely not” answer saves a disk trip altogether.
Cousins.







Filter
What it adds




Counting Bloom filter
Uses small counters instead of bits, so keys can be deleted (decrement)


Cuckoo filter
Built on cuckoo hashing, stores small fingerprints; supports insert and delete


SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
A compact immutable trie; answers range as well as point membership





Skip lists
The problem. The simplest ordered structure is a sorted linked list. It is easy to update, but search is \(O(n)\): you walk the whole thing.
The analogy. Think of a metro with express and local trains. The local train stops at every station, the express only at a few. To go far you ride the express, then switch to the local near your destination.
A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra “express lanes” stacked above it:

Level 0: every key, linked in order.
Level 1: roughly every other key.
Level 2: roughly every fourth key, and so on. Each level has about half the keys of the one below.







Figure 6: A skip list with three levels. Searching for 12 jumps along the express lane to 8, drops a level, jumps to 12, drops again, and is done.



Search. Start at the top-left. At each level go right while the next key is not larger than the target; when it would overshoot, drop down one level. This costs about \(O(\log n)\) on average, like a balanced tree.
Insert. Find the position on level 0 and insert there. Then flip a coin repeatedly to decide how many levels the new node also joins: heads, add it to the next level up; tails, stop. This randomness keeps the level sizes roughly halving without any rebalancing, which is the beauty of the structure: no global rebalancing, no node splitting.
Delete. Done in two phases: first logically delete by setting a flag on the node so that other threads skip it; later, physically unlink it once nobody could still hold a reference. This two-step approach is what makes lock-free implementations practical.







Pros
Cons




Simple; inserts and deletes touch only a few pointers
Not cache or disk friendly: nodes are scattered, no locality


No rebalancing
Reverse traversal is awkward (needs extra back pointers)


Easy to make concurrent
Each node carries several pointers, a memory cost



Because of the locality problem, skip lists are used mainly in memory. A well-known use is the memtable of LSM-tree storage engines, where recent writes are kept sorted in a skip list before being flushed to disk.


Tries and radix trees
The observation. A B+Tree’s inner keys cannot tell you whether a key exists. You must always go to the leaf. A trie (prefix tree, digital search tree) works differently: instead of comparing whole keys, it walks the key piece by piece.






Figure 7: The same three keys (HELLO, HAT, HAVE) in a trie and in a radix tree. The radix tree squashes chains of single-child nodes.



Properties of a trie:

The path from the root spells the key. The key is never stored whole: it is reconstructed from the path.
The shape depends only on the keys themselves, not on insertion order. So there is no rebalancing.
Cost is \(O(k)\), where \(k\) is the key length, regardless of how many keys are stored. (Compare to \(O(\log n)\) for a B+Tree.)
Shared prefixes (like HA above) are stored once.

Key span. Real tries do not go one letter at a time but one fixed-size digit at a time. The span is how many bits each level consumes.









Span
Fan-out per node
Levels for a 16-bit key
Trade-off




1 bit
2
16
Tiny nodes, very tall tree, slow


8 bits
256
2
Short tree, but a 256-slot node is wasteful if only a few children exist



Radix tree (Patricia tree). A vertically compressed trie: whenever a node has only one child, merge it into that child, so edges carry multi-character labels (Figure 7, right). This saves a lot of space on sparse keys. The catch: since skipped characters are not checked on the way down, a lookup can land on the wrong leaf. The DBMS therefore verifies the full key against the tuple at the end.
Modifications. Insert HAIR into the radix tree: the A node gets a new child IR. Delete HAT: its leaf disappears, and if that leaves a node with a single child, it is merged back into it (the compression is maintained).
Famous variants.








Variant
Where
Idea




Judy arrays
HP
256-way radix tree with adaptive node representations


ART (Adaptive Radix Tree)
HyPer
256-way radix tree whose node type adapts to how many children it has


Masstree
Silo
A B+Tree whose inside of each node is a trie


SuRF
CMU
A compressed static trie that is also a range filter





Inverted indexes
The problem. B+Trees answer “key = X” and “key between X and Y”. They are bad at content search:
SELECT pageID FROM revisions WHERE content LIKE '%Pavlo%';
A B+Tree is sorted by the beginning of the value. A word in the middle of a paragraph gives it nothing to navigate by, so the DBMS must scan every row.
The analogy. The index at the back of a textbook. Instead of “page 17 contains these words” (a forward map), it stores “this word appears on pages 17, 42, 88” (an inverted map). The idea is old: it was originally called a concordance, in use since the 1200s.






Figure 8: An inverted index. Each term in the dictionary points to a posting list of the documents that contain it. A multi-word query is answered by merging those lists.



It has two parts:

A dictionary: the sorted set of all terms (with, e.g., the document frequency \(df\)).
A posting list for each term: the sorted ids of records containing it (often with positions and counts).

cat AND dog is just an intersection of two sorted lists, a linear merge. cat OR dog is a union.
Real implementations.

Lucene (the engine inside Elasticsearch and Solr). The dictionary is stored as a finite state transducer (FST), like a trie that shares both prefixes and suffixes and maps a term to its offset, so it is extremely compact. The index is built as many small immutable segments, merged in the background. Posting lists use compression (delta encoding, bit packing) and can carry pre-computed stats.
PostgreSQL GIN (Generalized Inverted Index). The dictionary is a B+Tree. A term with few matches keeps a sorted list of record ids; a term with many matches gets its own B+Tree of record ids (a posting tree). Updates are expensive to apply one at a time, so GIN first appends them to a pending list and merges in batches.

Beyond exact words.

Ranking. Return the best matches first. The classic score is TF-IDF: a term is important in a document if it appears often there (term frequency) but rarely across the corpus (inverse document frequency):

\[
\text{tfidf}(t, d) = \text{tf}(t, d) \times \log\frac{N}{\text{df}(t)}
\]
BM25 refines this (it saturates the benefit of repeating a word and accounts for document length) and is the default in many search engines.

Tokenizers and n-grams. To support typos and autocomplete, split terms into overlapping fragments. The word database becomes the trigrams dat, ata, tab, aba, bas, ase. Now a misspelling like databse still shares most trigrams, so it still matches. (PostgreSQL’s pg_trgm and Elasticsearch’s n-gram tokenizer do exactly this.)
Normalization. Lower-casing and punctuation handling so that Wu-Tang matches Wu Tang.



Vector indexes
The problem. Inverted indexes match words. But sometimes you want meaning: “find albums with lyrics about running from the police,” even if none of them contains those exact words.
How it works.

A neural network (a transformer) turns each row’s text into an embedding: a long array of floating-point numbers (hundreds to thousands of dimensions). Texts with similar meaning land close together in this space.
At query time the query text is embedded by the same model.
The database finds the stored embeddings nearest to the query vector (by cosine or Euclidean distance) and returns their ids.

Queries often mix this with ordinary filters (“…and released after 2005”), so the DBMS has to decide whether to filter before or after the vector search. Also notice that the answer is approximate: correctness here means the result “feels right” rather than being exactly the true top-k. The quality is measured by recall: what fraction of the true nearest neighbours were found.
Exact nearest-neighbour search in hundreds of dimensions is hopeless to do faster than a full scan, so vector indexes trade a little accuracy for large speed-ups. Two families:

Approach 1: inverted-file (IVF) indexes
Partition the space into clusters, then only search the relevant ones. This is the same trick as the inverted index, with cluster centroids playing the role of words.






Figure 9: IVF. Vectors are grouped by their nearest centroid. A query is compared with centroids, then only the closest cluster(s) are scanned. Probing only one cluster can miss a neighbour just across the boundary.




Build: run k-means to find \(k\) centroids; assign every vector to the nearest centroid; build an inverted index centroid -> list of vectors.
Search: find the nearest centroid(s) to the query; scan only those lists.

Figure 9 shows the central weakness: points near a cluster boundary. The query’s closest centroid is C, but its closest vector lives in A. The fix is to probe several nearby clusters (nprobe): more recall, more work. Vectors are often compressed (“quantized”) to make the scans cheaper. IVFFlat in the pgvector extension is a well-known implementation.


Approach 2: graph indexes
Build a graph where every vector is a node connected to its (approximately) nearest neighbours. To search, start somewhere and greedily walk to whichever neighbour is closer to the query until no neighbour is closer. It is like finding a friend in a crowd by asking each person “who do you know that is closer to them?”
The best-known variant is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), which stacks several graph layers:






Figure 10: HNSW. The top layer is sparse, so each hop covers a long distance; lower layers are denser for fine-grained search. The query enters at the top and drops down a layer whenever it cannot get closer.



It is the same idea as the skip list from earlier: express lanes (sparse top layers) get you to the right neighbourhood quickly, and the dense bottom layer finishes the job. Implementations include Faiss, hnswlib and DiskANN (designed for graphs that do not fit in memory).









IVF
Graph (HNSW)




Idea
Cluster, then scan clusters
Walk a neighbour graph


Updates
Easier (add to a list)
Harder (rewire edges)


Speed/recall
Good; tuned via nprobe
Typically better at the same recall


Memory
Smaller

(The last two rows are general rules of thumb, not from the slides.)

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
The big picture
The lecture’s conclusion is blunt: the B+Tree is (almost) always a good choice. It is balanced, ordered, disk-friendly, handles range scans and has decades of engineering behind it. The other structures are specialists for narrower jobs.









Structure
Core idea
Best at
Weak at




B+Tree
Balanced tree, data in linked leaves
Point + range + ordered scans
Non-prefix content search


Bloom filter
Bit array + \(k\) hashes
Cheap “definitely not”
Deletes, locating data


Skip list
Linked lists with express lanes
In-memory ordered data, easy concurrency
Disk, cache locality


Trie / radix tree
Walk the key piece by piece
Prefix keys, \(O(k)\) lookup
Memory if sparse (hence radix/ART)


Inverted index
Term to list of records
Keyword / full-text search
Range queries, similarity


Vector index
Nearest neighbours of embeddings
“Find similar” queries
Exactness



And a few ideas recur across all of them, which I found the most useful takeaway:

Hierarchy to skip work. B+Tree levels, skip-list lanes and HNSW layers are all the same trick: take big steps first, small steps last.
Trade exactness for speed where the application allows it: Bloom filters (false positives) and vector indexes (approximate recall).
Batch to amortize cost: bulk loading, B-epsilon buffers and GIN’s pending list.
Everything is paged. Fanout, node size and pointer swizzling all come down to “how few pages does a lookup touch?”

title: Database Indexes: B+Trees, Skip Lists, Tries, Bloom Filters, Inverted and Vector Indexes
text:
Where to go next
The next lecture is the one I am most curious about: how to make these indexes thread-safe. Everything above assumed one thread at a time. Real systems have many threads splitting, merging and scanning the same tree simultaneously, which is where latches (from the buffer pool post) come back in.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
Watch the lecture this post is based on: CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems, Lecture 04: Buffer Pools (Prof. Andy Pavlo)
All the ideas here come from that lecture and its slides. The diagrams, examples and code are my own re-drawings, so any mistakes are mine.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
The problem in one sentence
A database can be far bigger than RAM, but it can only work on data that is in RAM. Something has to sit in the middle and decide:

which pages to pull into memory,
which pages to throw out when memory is full,
and when to write changed pages back to disk.

That something is the buffer pool manager. This post walks through how it works, why it is almost always a better manager than the operating system, and the replacement policies (LRU, Clock, LRU-K, ARC and friends) that decide who gets evicted. This blog is mostly a rambling ( with usage of claude to make me sound “legit” about my understanding of buffer pools in DBs in memory)

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
A desk and a library
The mental model I found most useful:

Disk is a huge library. It holds everything, but fetching a book takes a long walk.
Memory is your desk. It is small, but anything on it is instantly available.
The buffer pool is the desk management strategy: which books stay open, which go back to the shelf, and which you scribbled notes in (and therefore can’t just throw away).

Every decision in this lecture is a version of “the desk is full and I need space for one more book; what do I put back?”

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
Two kinds of control
The lecture frames the whole storage layer with two ideas:









Question it answers
Goal




Spatial control
Where on disk do we write pages?
Keep pages that are used together physically close, so reads are sequential.


Temporal control
When do we read pages into memory and write them back?
Minimize the number of times a query stalls waiting for disk.



Last lecture was mostly spatial (how pages are laid out in files). This lecture is temporal.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
section: How the buffer pool is organized
text:
How the buffer pool is organized
The buffer pool is just a big chunk of memory split into an array of fixed-size slots called frames. Each frame can hold exactly one page (same size as a disk page, commonly 4 KB to 16 KB depending on the system).






Figure 1: One request through the system: the execution engine asks the buffer pool for page 2. On a miss, the page is copied from disk into a free frame and a pointer to that frame is handed back.



Let’s trace what happens in Figure 1:

The execution engine says “I need page 2.”
The buffer pool checks whether page 2 is already in a frame. If not, it copies an exact copy of the page from disk into a free frame.
It returns a pointer to the frame. The engine reads or modifies the bytes directly in memory.

Notice what the engine never does: it never talks to the disk itself. Everything goes through the buffer pool.

Writes are lazy (write-back cache)
If a query modifies page 2, the DBMS does not write it to disk immediately. It modifies the in-memory copy and marks the frame as dirty. The write to disk happens later (on eviction, or by a background writer). This is called a write-back cache, and it is a big reason databases are fast: ten updates to the same page cost one disk write, not ten.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
section: The metadata that makes it work
text:
The metadata that makes it work
A frame by itself is just bytes. The buffer pool keeps extra bookkeeping so it can answer questions quickly.






Figure 2: The page table maps page ids to frames. Each frame carries metadata: a dirty flag, a pin counter, and access-tracking info used by the replacement policy.



The page table is an in-memory hash table: page_id -> frame. When someone asks for page 3, we hash, look it up, and either find the frame (a hit) or don’t (a miss).
Per-frame metadata:

Dirty flag. “This page was modified and the disk copy is stale.”
Pin / reference counter. “Someone is using this page right now.” A pinned page must never be evicted. Imagine a query is halfway through reading a page and the buffer pool yanks it away; that would be a disaster. Pin on the way in, unpin when done.
Access tracking info. Timestamps, reference bits, or access counts, whatever the replacement policy needs.

Putting it all together, here is the full life of a page request:






flowchart TD
    A["Engine asks for page 42"] --> B{"In page table?"}
    B -- "yes (hit)" --> C["Pin the frame, return pointer"]
    B -- "no (miss)" --> D{"Free frame?"}
    D -- "yes" --> G["Read page 42 from disk into the frame"]
    D -- "no" --> E["Pick a victim with the replacement policy (never a pinned frame)"]
    E --> F{"Victim dirty?"}
    F -- "yes (slow path)" --> H["Write victim to disk"]
    F -- "no (fast path)" --> I["Just drop it"]
    H --> I
    I --> G
    G --> C


 Life of a page request inside the buffer pool manager. 




Page table vs. page directory (easy to mix up)
These sound alike but are different things:









Page directory
Page table




Maps
page id -> location in the database files on disk
page id -> frame in the buffer pool


Lives
On disk (must survive restart)
In memory only (rebuilt from nothing after a restart)





Locks vs. latches
Another pair of words people conflate. Many threads hit the page table at the same time, so it needs protection, but not with the same thing that protects your rows.









Lock
Latch




Protects
Logical database contents (rows, tables) from other transactions
Internal data structures (like the page table) from other threads


Held for
The duration of a transaction
The duration of a single operation (microseconds)


Rollback needed?
Yes
No



A latch is basically a mutex. Think of a lock as “don’t touch my row” and a latch as “don’t touch this hash table while I’m halfway through updating it.”


The buffer pool isn’t the only memory pool
The DBMS uses memory for lots of other things too, and these may or may not be backed by disk: sort and join buffers, query caches, maintenance buffers, log buffers, dictionary caches. This lecture is about the one that caches table and index pages.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
“Why not just use the OS?” (mmap)
This is the question every student asks, so let’s take it seriously.
mmap lets a program map a file into its address space. You then read and write the file as if it were a plain array in memory, and the OS handles moving pages between disk and RAM. No buffer pool to write. Sounds perfect.
The trouble starts when the file is bigger than RAM and you have multiple threads. The OS decides which pages stay and which go, and it knows nothing about your queries.
The lecture lists the problems:

Transaction safety. The OS can flush a dirty page to disk at any moment, including before the matching log record is written. That breaks the rule that the log must hit disk first (write-ahead logging).
I/O stalls. The DBMS doesn’t know which pages are in memory. A touch on an evicted page triggers a page fault and the OS silently blocks your thread while it reads from disk. The DBMS can’t do something smarter in the meantime.
Error handling. With a buffer pool you can validate a page after reading it and handle failures right there. With mmap, any memory access can fail with a SIGBUS signal that you have to handle.
Performance issues. Contention on OS-internal data structures and costly TLB shootdowns when many threads are involved.

“But Linux gives me knobs!” It does:

madvise: hint how you’ll access a range of pages.
mlock: pin a range in memory so it can’t be paged out.
msync: force a range to be flushed to disk.

The lecture’s point is that using these to coax the OS into behaving is just as much work as managing memory yourself, and you still get less control.
What the DBMS can do better than the OS, because it knows the query plan:

flush dirty pages in the correct order,
do specialized prefetching,
choose a smarter replacement policy,
do its own thread scheduling.

The lecture’s slogan is “the OS is not your friend.” (The paper it points to is Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System? from CIDR 2022, linked in the references below.)

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
Replacement policies: who gets evicted?
The buffer pool is full and a new page is needed. Which frame do we reuse? A good policy is judged on:

Correctness. Never evict a pinned page.
Accuracy. Evict pages you won’t need soon.
Speed. Picking a victim shouldn’t be slow.
Metadata overhead. Tracking shouldn’t eat too much memory.


LRU: Least Recently Used (1965)
The idea is that a page used recently will likely be used again soon, so evict the one touched longest ago. Keep pages in an ordered list; every access moves the page to the “newest” end; evict from the “oldest” end.
A quick trace with a pool of 3 frames (oldest on the left):



Access
Result
Pool (oldest -> newest)




A
miss
A


B
miss
A B


C
miss
A B C


A
hit (A moves to newest)
B C A


D
miss, evict B (oldest)
C A D



Simple and intuitive. It has one nasty weakness, which we will get to shortly.


Clock (1969): LRU on a budget
Keeping an exact timestamp ordering for every page is expensive. Clock approximates LRU with just one bit per page.

Each page has a reference bit. Whenever the page is accessed, set it to 1.
Pages sit in a circle with a “clock hand”.
To find a victim, sweep the hand: if the bit is 1, set it to 0 and move on (a second chance). If the bit is 0, evict it.







Figure 3: A Clock snapshot: pages 1, 3 and 4 were touched since the last sweep, page 2 was not. The hand clears three bits and then evicts page 2.



In Figure 3 the hand starts at page 1 (bit 1, so it’s cleared), then page 3 (cleared), then page 4 (cleared), and finally page 2 has bit 0, so page 2 is evicted. A page only survives if it was touched since the last time the hand passed by.
Cheap, no sorting, no timestamps. That’s why variants of Clock show up in real systems.


The weakness: sequential flooding
LRU and Clock share a blind spot. Imagine this workload with a pool of 3 frames and a table of 6 pages:

Q1: SELECT * FROM A WHERE id = 1 reads page 0 (a “hot” page we use constantly).
Q2: SELECT AVG(val) FROM A scans every page, 0 to 5, once.
Q3: SELECT * FROM A WHERE id = 1 again, wants page 0.




Access
Result
Pool (oldest -> newest)




Q1: p0
miss
0


Q2: p0
hit
0


Q2: p1
miss
0 1


Q2: p2
miss
0 1 2


Q2: p3
miss, evict p0
1 2 3


Q2: p4
miss, evict p1
2 3 4


Q2: p5
miss, evict p2
3 4 5


Q3: p0
miss, p0 was flushed out by the scan
4 5 0



The scan pushed out the one page we actually cared about, and replaced it with pages (3, 4, 5) that will never be read again. That’s sequential flooding: a scan pollutes the buffer pool with read-once pages.
It gets worse with loops. If a query repeatedly scans 4 pages in a loop with a 3-frame pool, LRU always evicts the page that will be needed next. I ran a quick simulation of 12 accesses (three passes over pages 0 to 3):



Policy
Hits out of 12




LRU
0


MRU (evict most recently used)
6



That’s the lecture’s observation: in many analytical (OLAP) workloads, the most recently used page is often the best one to evict. The DBMS knows it is doing a scan, so it should act accordingly. We’ll see how below.


LFU: Least Frequently Used (1971)
If “recent” isn’t enough, count how often a page is accessed and evict the lowest count. That recognizes that the hot page 0 above is touched a lot.
But LFU has its own problems:

Keeping pages ordered by count costs logarithmic time relative to the cache size.
It ignores time. A page that was hammered last week has a huge count and sits in memory forever, even if nobody wants it anymore.



LRU-K (1993): use the history
LRU only looks at the last access. LRU-K remembers the last K access timestamps for each page, and uses the K-th most recent one to estimate when the page will be used next. The score is the backward distance:
\[
\text{backward distance} = \text{current time} - K\text{-th most recent access}
\]
Pages with fewer than K accesses have an infinite backward distance, so they are evicted first (oldest first-access breaks ties). That is exactly what prevents one-time scan pages from kicking out genuinely popular pages.
A small example with K = 2 and 3 frames. The pool holds A, B, C, and page D now arrives at time 5:



Time
Access

Both B and C have infinite distance; the earlier first access is B, so B is evicted. Plain LRU would have picked A (last touched at t2, the oldest) even though A is the only page touched more than once. LRU-K protects it.
The lecture also mentions keeping an in-memory ghost cache of recently evicted pages’ history, so a page that was just evicted doesn’t instantly lose all the evidence that it mattered.


MySQL’s approximate LRU-K
True LRU-K is somewhat heavy, so MySQL (InnoDB) approximates it with a neat trick: one linked list with two entry points.






Figure 4: MySQL’s approximation. New pages enter at the head of the OLD part. Only when they are accessed a second time do they get promoted to the head of the YOUNG part.




A brand-new page is inserted at the head of the old section, not the front of the whole list.
If it’s touched again while in the old section, it gets promoted to the head of the young section.
Evictions come from the tail of the old section.

So a page read once by a big scan drifts through the old section and gets evicted without ever disturbing the young, proven-popular pages. A page that gets accessed twice earns its place. That’s “K = 2” behavior with just a linked list. (In InnoDB the old section is roughly the last 3/8 of the list by default; it’s tunable.)


ARC: Adaptive Replacement Cache (2003)
What if the best balance between “recent” and “frequent” changes with the workload? ARC (from IBM Research) learns it on the fly. The lecture notes it’s used in IBM DB2 and ZFS, and PostgreSQL had a rewritten version to avoid IBM’s patent.
It maintains four lists:

T1 (recent): pages seen exactly once recently.
T2 (frequent): pages seen at least twice.
B1 (ghost of T1): only the ids of pages recently evicted from T1.
B2 (ghost of T2): only the ids of pages recently evicted from T2.
And a target parameter p that says how much of the cache to give to T1 vs T2.







Figure 5: ARC. Real pages live in T1 and T2. The ghost lists remember what was just evicted, and a hit in a ghost list tells ARC which side it was too stingy to.



The clever part is the ghost lists. Suppose you ask for page X, it’s not in memory, but its id is in B1. That means “I evicted X from the recent list, and I needed it again shortly after.” The recent side was too small, so ARC increases p (more room for recency). A hit in B2 says the opposite: the frequent side was too small, so decrease p.






flowchart TD
    A["Request page X"] --> B{"Where is X?"}
    B -- "in T1" --> C["Hit: promote T1 to T2 (now 'frequent')"]
    B -- "in T2" --> D["Hit: stays in T2"]
    B -- "in ghost B1" --> E["Miss: increase p, load X into T2"]
    B -- "in ghost B2" --> F["Miss: decrease p, load X into T2"]
    B -- "nowhere" --> G["Miss: make room (evict from T1/B1 or T2/B2), insert X into T1"]


 ARC lookup, simplified from the lecture’s protocol. 



A page lives in only one list at a time. Anything new goes into T1; touching it again moves it to T2. So a one-time scan only ever occupies T1 and can’t flush the frequent set in T2.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
section: Smarter policies using what the DBMS knows
text:
Smarter policies using what the DBMS knows
LRU, Clock, ARC all just watch accesses. The DBMS has much more information because it knows the query plan. Two ways to use it:

Localization
Evict on a per-query basis so one query can’t pollute the whole pool. Postgres, for example, gives a scan a small, limited ring of buffer pool pages and reuses it as a circular buffer. A big sequential scan keeps recycling its own ring and leaves everyone else’s pages alone.


Priority hints
The DBMS can tell the buffer pool “this page is important.” Say the table has an index on id, and the workload is:

INSERT INTO A VALUES (id++): always appends at the right edge of the B+tree.
SELECT * FROM A WHERE id = ?: a lookup, which must start at the root of the tree.

The root and the right-most leaf are obviously worth keeping resident. The upper index pages get high priority, a random leaf gets low. No generic replacement policy can know that, but the query executor can.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
section: Dirty pages: fast path vs slow path
text:
Dirty pages: fast path vs slow path
When we pick a victim:

Not dirty means a fast path: just drop it. The disk already has the same bytes.
Dirty means a slow path: write it to disk first, then reuse the frame.

There’s a trade-off: preferring clean victims makes eviction fast, but you might evict a page that’s about to be read again just because it was clean.

Background writing
To avoid slow-path evictions in the hot path, the DBMS runs a background writer (aka page cleaner or buffer flusher) that periodically walks the page table and writes dirty pages to disk. After a safe flush, the page can be evicted instantly, or just have its dirty flag reset.
The catch: you can’t flush a dirty page before its log record has been written (write-ahead logging, which comes in a later lecture). Background writing must respect that.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
section: Taking disk I/O away from the OS
text:
Taking disk I/O away from the OS

I/O scheduling
The OS and disk hardware reorder and batch I/O requests to maximize bandwidth, but they cannot tell which requests matter more. The DBMS keeps its own queues and prioritizes by:

sequential vs. random I/O,
critical-path work vs. background work,
table vs. index vs. log vs. temporary data,
transaction information,
user-based SLAs.

That’s why many databases (Oracle, Vertica, MySQL) advise switching Linux to a simple deadline or noop (FIFO) I/O scheduler: let the DBMS be the smart one.


The OS page cache and O_DIRECT
Even when you use plain read()/write(), the OS keeps its own cache of file pages (the page cache). Your data then lives in memory twice: once in the OS cache and once in your buffer pool. And the two caches have different eviction policies.






flowchart LR
    subgraph U["User space"]
        D["DBMS buffer pool"]
    end
    subgraph K["Kernel space"]
        C["OS page cache"]
    end
    X[("Disk")]
    D -- "read()" --> C
    C --> X
    D -. "O_DIRECT bypasses the cache" .-> X


 Without O_DIRECT, reads go through the kernel’s page cache and the data is cached twice. 



Most DBMSs therefore open files with O_DIRECT, which skips the OS cache and avoids redundant copies, conflicting policies, and loss of control over file I/O.


The fsync horror story
Here’s why “the OS is not your friend” isn’t just a slogan:

fwrite only writes into the OS cache. It does not mean the data is on disk.
fsync asks the OS to flush it to disk.
What if fsync fails with an I/O error (EIO)? On Linux, the dirty pages get marked clean, and the next fsync call happily reports success.

A DBMS that retries fsync after a failure and trusts the success may believe data is safely on disk when it was actually lost. Lesson: if fsync fails, treat it as fatal; don’t retry and assume.

title: The Buffer Pool: How a Database Decides What Lives in Memory
text:
The big picture
The conclusion of the lecture fits in two lines:

The DBMS can almost always manage memory better than the OS, because it knows what’s coming.
Use the semantics of the query plan to make better decisions about evictions, allocations and prefetching.

A cheat sheet:








Policy / technique
Core idea
Fixes / helps with




LRU
Evict the least recently touched page
Basic temporal locality


Clock
One reference bit and a sweeping hand
LRU’s metadata cost


LFU
Evict the least frequently used
Popularity, but ignores age


LRU-K
Use the K-th last access
Sequential flooding


MySQL young/old
One list, two entry points
Cheap LRU-2 behavior


ARC
Recent + frequent lists with ghosts, self-tuning
Shifting workloads


Localization
Per-query frame budget
One query polluting the pool


Priority hints
Executor marks important pages
Index roots, hot pages

Where to go next
I will be uploading another blog possibly on On disk storage, that deals with the pages, layouts, page directory and much more. That could potentially be a longer blog.
